Part 1: Boundary Extraction¶

Load the leaf image

Perform boundary extraction

Display the extracted boundary image and original image side by side

In [1]:
#load in all libraries for the lab
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import cv2
from google.colab.patches import cv2_imshow
from PIL import Image, ImageFilter
In [2]:
#load in leaf png
leaf = cv2.imread('leaf.png', cv2.IMREAD_GRAYSCALE)

#boundary extraction
#Convert to binary
_, leaf_binary = cv2.threshold(leaf, 127, 255, cv2.THRESH_BINARY)
#Define the kernel
kernel = np.ones((3,3), np.uint8)
#Perform dilation
leaf_dilated = cv2.dilate(leaf_binary, kernel, iterations=1)
#Perform erosion
leaf_eroded = cv2.erode(leaf_binary, kernel, iterations=1)
#Outer Boundary
outer_boundary = cv2.subtract(leaf_dilated, leaf_binary)
#Inner Boundary
inner_boundary = cv2.subtract(leaf_binary, leaf_eroded)

#Plot original, outer, and inner side by side
fig, axs = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(15, 5))
axs[0].imshow(leaf, cmap='gray')
axs[0].set_title('Original')
axs[1].imshow(outer_boundary, cmap='gray')
axs[1].set_title('Outer Boundary')
axs[2].imshow(inner_boundary, cmap='gray')
axs[2].set_title('Inner Boundary')
plt.show()

Part 2: Closing¶

Load image 2 and perform closing operation, but use PIL library

Display the original and closed image side by side

In [3]:
#load image using PIL
image2 = Image.open('image 2.png')
#convert to RGB
image2 = image2.convert('RGB')
#convert to grayscale
image2 = image2.convert('L')
#convert to binary
binary_image2 = image2.point(lambda p:p > 127 and 255)
#convert to numpy array
binary_image2_array = np.array(binary_image2)
#perform closing operation using PIL
#Perform dilation
binary_image2_dilated = Image.fromarray(binary_image2_array).filter(ImageFilter.MaxFilter(3))
binary_image2_dilated = np.array(binary_image2_dilated)
#Perform erosion
binary_image2_eroded = Image.fromarray(binary_image2_dilated).filter(ImageFilter.MinFilter(3))
binary_image2_closed = np.array(binary_image2_eroded)

#Plot original next to closed img
fig, axs = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(15, 5))
axs[0].imshow(binary_image2, cmap='gray')
axs[0].set_title('Original')
axs[1].imshow(binary_image2_closed, cmap='gray')
axs[1].set_title('Closed')
axs[0].axis('off')
axs[1].axis('off')
plt.show()

Part 3: Region Filling 1¶

Load the gray_coins image and perform region filling on the image

After performing region filling, perform some operation and that leads to coin output image 1

Display both images side by side

In [4]:
#Read in gray coins png
gray_coins = cv2.imread('gray coins.png', cv2.IMREAD_GRAYSCALE)
#convert to binary
_, gray_coins_binary = cv2.threshold(gray_coins, 127, 255, cv2.THRESH_BINARY)
#Define function similar to the one in the module
def region_filling(image, seed_point):
  h,w = image.shape
  F = np.zeros((h,w), dtype=np.uint8)
  F[seed_point] = 1
  boundary_complement = cv2.bitwise_not(image)
  structuring_element = cv2.getStructuringElement(cv2.MORPH_CROSS, (3,3))
  while True:
    F_dilated = cv2.dilate(F, structuring_element)
    F_new = cv2.bitwise_and(F_dilated, boundary_complement)
    if np.array_equal(F_new, F):
      break
    F = F_new
  filled_image = cv2.bitwise_or(image, F)
  return filled_image

#Perform region filling
filled_image = region_filling(gray_coins_binary, (10,10))

#plot original next to filled
fig, axs = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(15, 5))
axs[0].imshow(gray_coins, cmap='gray')
axs[0].set_title('Original')
axs[1].imshow(filled_image, cmap='gray')
axs[1].set_title('Filled')
axs[0].axis('off')
axs[1].axis('off')
plt.show()
In [5]:
#Perform more cleaning to try to match the coins output 1 that was provided
#load in coins output 1
coins_output_1 = cv2.imread('coin output image1.png', cv2.IMREAD_GRAYSCALE)

#Perform morphological closing to get rid of more of the black
#Started with (3,3) and increased until it matched
kernel = np.ones((9,9), np.uint8)
filled_image_changed = cv2.morphologyEx(filled_image, cv2.MORPH_CLOSE, kernel)

#plot coins output 1 and new filled image
fig, axs = plt.subplots(1,2, figsize=(15,5))
axs[0].imshow(coins_output_1, cmap='gray')
axs[0].set_title('Coins Output 1')
axs[1].imshow(filled_image_changed, cmap='gray')
axs[1].set_title('New Filled Image')
axs[0].axis('off')
axs[1].axis('off')
plt.show()

Part 5: Connected Components¶

Load the squares image and apply the connected components algorithm on it

Print the number of connected components

Can you explain how and why the number is, what it is?

In [7]:
#Load the squares image
squares = cv2.imread('squares.png', cv2.IMREAD_GRAYSCALE)
#convert to binary
_, squares_binary = cv2.threshold(squares, 127, 255, cv2.THRESH_BINARY)
#get number of labels
num_labels, labels_im = cv2.connectedComponents(squares_binary)
#print number of connected components
print("Number of connected components: ", num_labels)
print('\n')
#Apply connected component via function similar to module
def imshow_components(labels):
    # Map component labels to hue val
    label_hue = np.uint8(179*labels/np.max(labels))
    blank_ch = 255*np.ones_like(label_hue)
    labeled_img = cv2.merge([label_hue, blank_ch, blank_ch])

    #convert to BGR for display
    labeled_img = cv2.cvtColor(labeled_img, cv2.COLOR_HSV2BGR)

    #set bg label to black
    labeled_img[label_hue==0] = 0

    cv2_imshow(labeled_img)

#Apply to squares
imshow_components(labels_im)

Number of connected components:  14

Explanation of Number of Connected Components¶

There are 14 components because the algorithm found items where the pixels were the same when checking around it which led to some of the squares being grouped together¶
